AI.method: Geometric approach using principal angles between subspaces for fault isolability; hybrid estimator combining a Luenberger-like observer with contraction guarantees; neural networks embedded in the observer for fault estimation; mirror descent-based adaptive laws for online adaptation of the last network layer to enforce isolability conditions without assuming a quadratic parameter space.
AI.result: Lyapunov-based analysis proves that state and parameter estimation errors are uniformly ultimately bounded. Effectiveness is demonstrated on a 3-axis spacecraft attitude control system.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FDI method successfully handles simultaneous actuator and sensor faults in nonlinear control-affine systems, with rigorous stability guarantees and empirical validation on a spacecraft attitude control system.

title: Replicating Real-World 23-Hz Oscillations Caused by Large Electronic Loads
summary: In 2024, Texas operators observed 23-Hz oscillations in real power measurements close to a large electronic load (LEL). Oscillations emerged when the load's power consumption reached approximately 320 MW level and subsided as the active power demand decreased. The paper aims to analyze the event and reproduce the oscillations using electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations. In the first stage, a representative feedback system is developed, and frequency-domain analysis is conducted to examine the phenomenon and identify its key influencing factors. Next, detailed EMT simulations are performed to further validate the proposed analytical approach. The results show that the feedback system effectively captures and characterizes the critical features of the 23-Hz oscillation incident. In addition, the EMT simulations successfully reproduce the real-world event, with the simulated results closely matching the fault recorder data.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 23-Hz oscillations observed in Texas power measurements near a large electronic load, develops a feedback system model and frequency-domain analysis, validates findings with EMT simulations that closely match real-world fault recorder data.
AI.motivation: To analyze and understand the 23-Hz oscillations observed in real power measurements near a large electronic load in Texas, which emerged when load reached ~320 MW and subsided with decreased demand.
AI.method: First, a representative feedback system was developed with frequency-domain analysis to examine the phenomenon and identify key influencing factors. Then, detailed EMT simulations were performed to validate the analytical approach.
AI.result: The feedback system effectively captures and characterizes critical features of the 23-Hz oscillation. EMT simulations successfully reproduce the real-world event, with results closely matching fault recorder data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed analytical approach and EMT simulations can accurately reproduce and characterize the 23-Hz oscillation incident involving large electronic loads.

title: Revisiting the Voltage-Source Behavior: Why Impedance Magnitude of Grid-Forming Converter Rises Near Fundamental Frequency?
summary: Grid-forming (GFM) converters are generally expected to exhibit low impedance near the fundamental frequency due to their voltage-source behavior. However, an impedance peak and a negative-resistance region are consistently observed in this range, which contradicts this expectation and lacks a clear physical explanation. This paper reveals that these phenomena originate from the inherent dynamics of the active power control loop, where the mapping from power disturbance to the synchronous angle inherently involves an integrative action, intrinsically preventing a positive-resistance characteristic near the fundamental frequency. This finding explains why existing grid codes in China, the United States, and Europe exclude a narrow band around the fundamental frequency in impedance-based evaluations. It is further shown that the width of the excluded frequency band (e.g., +/- 3~5 Hz) is governed by the power-to-frequency dynamics. Based on this insight, a quantitative index is proposed to determine the exclusion bandwidth from the corner frequencies of the impedance magnitude curve. The proposed index provides a concise and theoretically grounded criterion for voltage-source assessment and impedance standardization of GFM converters.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that grid-forming converters inherently exhibit an impedance peak and negative-resistance region near the fundamental frequency due to the integrative dynamics of active power control loops. It explains why grid codes exclude a narrow band around the fundamental frequency and proposes a quantitative index to determine the exclusion bandwidth based on impedance magnitude corner frequencies.
AI.motivation: Grid-forming converters are expected to have low impedance near the fundamental frequency due to voltage-source behavior, but an impedance peak and negative-resistance region are consistently observed without clear physical explanation. The paper aims to reveal the root cause and provide a theoretical basis for existing grid code practices.
AI.method: The paper analytically investigates the active power control loop dynamics, showing that the mapping from power disturbance to synchronous angle inherently involves integrative action. It derives the relationship between the excluded frequency band width and power-to-frequency dynamics, and proposes a quantitative index based on corner frequencies of the impedance magnitude curve.
AI.result: The negative-resistance characteristic near the fundamental frequency is intrinsically caused by the integrative nature of active power control. The exclusion bandwidth (e.g., ±3–5 Hz) observed in grid codes is governed by power-to-frequency dynamics. A quantitative index is derived to determine this bandwidth from impedance magnitude corner frequencies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed index provides a concise, theoretically grounded criterion for voltage-source assessment and impedance standardization of GFM converters, offering clear guidance for grid code development.

title: Handling Control System Uncertainty
summary: Control science is a core representative of the third industrial revolution and is so important to modern civilization. Control systems are the main subject of control science and may involve many aspects of consideration, such as hardware consideration, software consideration, operation consideration, maintenance consideration, economy consideration, society consideration. However, besides all such aspects of consideration, one aspect that is most essential to the control system is methodology consideration in mathematical sense, knowledge on which is what we refer to as control theory. Besides its importance from the mathematical perspective, control theory is even more charming as it is deeply rooted in practical applications. Charms of control theory consist in both know-why and know-how and it is the fusion of control theory and practical applications that highlights such charms. Control theory for practical applications, especially when somewhat with so-called ``advanced'' flavour, involves several fundamental aspects. This article introduces the Handling Control System Uncertainty aspect of Advanced Control Theory for Practical Applications.

AI.tldr: Control theory is essential to modern civilization as the methodological core of control systems, combining mathematical rigor with practical application, with a specific focus on handling uncertainty in advanced control for real-world use.
AI.motivation: To highlight the fundamental importance of control theory as the methodological core of control systems, and to introduce the specific aspect of handling uncertainty in advanced control theory for practical applications.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis and exposition of control theory's role, distinguishing between various aspects of control systems (hardware, software, economics, etc.) and emphasizing methodology in the mathematical sense as the most essential aspect.
AI.result: Identifies handling control system uncertainty as a fundamental aspect of advanced control theory for practical applications.
AI.conclusion: Control theory's charm lies in the fusion of know-why and know-how, and handling uncertainty is a key aspect of advanced control theory applied in practice.

title: Latency-Aware Deep Learning Benchmark for Real-Time Cyber-Physical Attack and Fault Classification in Inverter-Dominated Power Grids
summary: This work introduces a latency-aware benchmarking framework for evaluating deep learning models in power system anomaly detection using high-fidelity, time-domain signals generated from an industry-grade electromagnetic transient simulator. Eight neural network architectures, ranging from MLPs to Transformers, were systematically evaluated on streaming datasets representing both physical faults and cyber-attacks in inverter-dominated networks. All models successfully classified two representative multi-event sequences in real time with sub-cycle response times below 15 ms. However, although classification decisions occurred within one cycle, the end-to-end inference latency consistently exceeded three cycles, ranging from 50 to 90 ms. These results highlight a critical gap between algorithmic capability and protection-grade deployment, pointing to the need for further optimization and hardware acceleration. The findings establish a reproducible benchmark for sub-cycle anomaly detection and provide guidance for transitioning machine learning methods from research prototypes to real-world protection applications.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a latency-aware benchmarking framework for deep learning models in power system anomaly detection using high-fidelity simulated data. While all eight tested architectures (MLPs to Transformers) achieved sub-cycle classification decisions (<15ms), the end-to-end inference latency (50-90ms) consistently exceeded three cycles, revealing a gap between algorithmic capability and protection-grade deployment requirements. The work provides a reproducible benchmark and guidance for transitioning ML methods to real-world protection applications.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between deep learning model performance and real-world protection-grade deployment in power system anomaly detection by systematically evaluating the latency characteristics of various neural network architectures under realistic, streaming conditions.
AI.method: A latency-aware benchmarking framework was developed using high-fidelity, time-domain signals from an industry-grade electromagnetic transient simulator. Eight neural network architectures (MLPs to Transformers) were evaluated on streaming datasets representing physical faults and cyber-attacks in inverter-dominated networks, with a focus on classification speed and end-to-end inference latency.
AI.result: All models achieved sub-cycle classification decisions (<15ms) for two multi-event sequences. However, end-to-end inference latency ranged from 50-90ms, consistently exceeding three power system cycles, highlighting a critical gap between raw model speed and practical deployment constraints.
AI.conclusion: There exists a significant gap between algorithmic classification capability and protection-grade deployment requirements, necessitating further optimization and hardware acceleration. The work establishes a reproducible benchmark and offers guidance for transitioning machine learning methods from research to real-world protection applications.

title: Distributed 3D Leader-Follower Formation Control with Field-of-View Safety via Control Barrier Functions
summary: This letter proposes a distributed 3D leader-follower formation (3D-LFF) control framework for multi-UAV systems that achieves formation tracking while enforcing perception safety constraints. Maintaining safe, vision-based 3D-LFF is challenging because onboard cameras impose strict Field-of-View (FOV) limitations, and demanding formation commands can drive the leader outside the follower's camera frustum, resulting in loss of visibility. To address this issue, we develop a perception-aware safe control architecture that guarantees visibility by construction. First, we derive a relative kinematic model in a line-of-sight coordinate representation and design a distributed 3D-LFF tracking controller using only locally available relative states. Next, we embed the nominal formation controller within a Control Barrier Function-based Quadratic Program (CBF-QP) safety filter that minimally modifies the commanded velocities to maintain the leader inside the follower's camera frustum while preserving formation tracking whenever feasible. Gazebo simulations and Crazyflie hardware experiments validate the proposed approach, demonstrating accurate formation tracking and effective FOV enforcement, including scenarios in which the nominal desired formation conflicts with visibility constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a distributed 3D leader-follower formation control framework for multi-UAV systems that uses Control Barrier Functions to enforce camera Field-of-View constraints, ensuring the leader remains visible within the follower's camera frustum while maintaining formation tracking. Validated via Gazebo simulations and Crazyflie hardware experiments.
AI.motivation: Maintaining safe, vision-based 3D leader-follower formation control for multi-UAV systems is challenging because onboard cameras impose strict Field-of-View (FOV) limitations, and demanding formation commands can drive the leader outside the follower's camera frustum, resulting in loss of visibility and potential mission failure.
AI.method: The authors derive a relative kinematic model in line-of-sight coordinate representation, design a distributed 3D-LFF tracking controller using only locally available relative states, and embed it within a CBF-QP safety filter that minimally modifies commanded velocities to keep the leader inside the follower's camera frustum while preserving formation tracking when feasible.
AI.result: Gazebo simulations and Crazyflie hardware experiments demonstrate accurate formation tracking and effective FOV enforcement, including scenarios where the nominal desired formation conflicts with visibility constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed perception-aware safe control architecture guarantees visibility by construction, resolving the fundamental conflict between formation tracking and camera FOV limitations in vision-based multi-UAV systems.

title: Distributed Synchronisation of Heterogeneous Dynamical Networks With Nonlinear Diffusive Couplings
summary: This letter investigates the problem of output synchronisation in heterogeneous dynamical networks with nonlinear diffusive couplings in the presence of disturbances on the coupling links. By exploiting relative dissipativity properties between adjacent agents, distributed conditions are established to guarantee output synchronisation. Specifically, these conditions can be verified using only local information associated with neighbouring agents and coupling links. As an illustration, a heterogeneous network of Goodwin oscillators is considered, where the relative dissipativity properties between neighbouring oscillators are characterised and used to analyse synchronisation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies output synchronization in heterogeneous dynamical networks with nonlinear diffusive couplings and disturbances on coupling links, using relative dissipativity between agents to establish distributed conditions verified locally, demonstrated on a network of Goodwin oscillators.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of output synchronization in heterogeneous networks with nonlinear diffusive couplings and disturbances on coupling links, which cannot be handled by existing methods relying on absolute dissipativity or disturbance-free assumptions.
AI.method: Exploits relative dissipativity properties between adjacent agents to derive distributed synchronization conditions that can be verified using only local information from neighboring agents and coupling links.
AI.result: Established distributed conditions for output synchronization that are verifiable with local information; successfully characterized relative dissipativity between neighboring Goodwin oscillators to analyze synchronization.
AI.conclusion: Relative dissipativity provides a viable framework for distributed output synchronization in heterogeneous nonlinear networks with disturbances, with the Goodwin oscillator case confirming the approach's applicability.

title: Distributed Synthesis of Gray-Box Distributed H2 Controllers
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 23rd IFAC World Congress, Busan, South Korea, 2026
summary: Distributed controller synthesis offers scalable and privacy-preserving control design, but typical state-of-the-art approaches either assume white-box models or resort to centralized synthesis. In this paper, we combine partially known model knowledge and an input-state dataset within a distributed gray-box scheme to design \(\mathcal{H}_2\) controllers. Our method can handle unknown dynamics and offers scalable synthesis. Each agent communicates with a set of neighbors determined by the physical coupling topology of the system such that we can apply the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to solve the problem iteratively in a fully distributed fashion (i.e., without a central server). The effectiveness and flexibility of the proposed approach is demonstrated in simulations of the IEEE 39-bus power system test case.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a distributed gray-box scheme for synthesizing H₂ controllers that combines partially known model knowledge with input-state data, using ADMM to solve the problem iteratively without a central server, demonstrated on an IEEE 39-bus power system.
AI.motivation: Distributed controller synthesis faces a trade-off: existing approaches either assume white-box models (requiring full system knowledge) or resort to centralized synthesis (compromising scalability and privacy). The authors aim to overcome this gap by enabling scalable, privacy-preserving control design that works with partially unknown dynamics.
AI.method: The approach combines partially known model knowledge with an input-state dataset in a distributed gray-box scheme. Communication is restricted to physical coupling-determined neighbors, enabling the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to solve the H₂ controller synthesis problem iteratively in a fully distributed manner without a central coordinator.
AI.result: The effectiveness and flexibility of the approach are validated through simulations on the IEEE 39-bus power system test case.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully handles unknown dynamics while maintaining scalable, fully distributed synthesis, offering a practical middle ground between white-box and centralized approaches.

title: Architecture Dependent Temporal Observability Under Deployment Interference in Edge Inference Systems
summary:
Edge inference systems are typically evaluated with software-reported latency collected under controlled conditions. We argue, and demonstrate empirically, that deployment interference can corrupt not only the inference timing being measured but the timing observability infrastructure that measures it, and that the two failures can occur independently.
  We pair software-reported timing with externally observable GPIO intervals captured by a Saleae Logic Pro 8 logic analyzer on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, running MobileNetV2 under two inference architectures (TensorRT FP16 GPU and ONNX Runtime CPU) across baseline, light memory pressure, and storage writeback stress. Across 35 paired capture runs (3500 samples) plus 3 storage-stress runs where external pairing failed (300 software-only samples), we observe three findings the software-only view does not surface. (1) The two architectures differ not only in mean latency but in distributional structure: TensorRT baseline clusters tightly near 1.23 ms (run-mean SD 15 us) while ORT CPU baseline is multimodal with run-mean SD 31.8 ms. (2) Light memory pressure inflates TensorRT P99 from 1.28 ms to 1.61 ms, while one of five ORT memory-stress runs collapses into a deterministic 198 ms regime rather than uniformly inflating variance. (3) All three TensorRT storage-stress runs produce complete software timing logs (100/100 iterations) alongside externally observable timing failures of three different kinds (full post-marker collapse, ~40% transition loss, and complete acquisition failure) -- while the runtime reports normal completion in every case.
  We claim, narrowly, that timing observability is itself an interference-sensitive resource, and that summary statistics from a single timing source can hide failure modes an independent external observer makes visible.

AI.tldr: Edge inference timing observability is itself susceptible to deployment interference, and software-reported latency can mask failures that an independent external observer (logic analyzer) reveals, demonstrated across 3500+ samples on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano running MobileNetV2 under TensorRT and ONNX Runtime.
AI.motivation: Standard edge inference evaluations rely on software-reported latency under controlled conditions, but deployment interference might corrupt both the timing being measured and the observability infrastructure itself—potentially hiding failures that a single timing source cannot detect.
AI.method: Paired software-reported timing (TensorRT FP16 GPU and ONNX Runtime CPU) with externally observable GPIO intervals from a Saleae Logic Pro 8 logic analyzer on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano running MobileNetV2 under baseline, light memory pressure, and storage writeback stress. 35 paired runs (3500 samples) plus 3 storage-stress runs where external pairing failed (300 software-only samples).
AI.result: (1) TensorRT baseline clusters tightly near 1.23 ms (SD 15 us) while ORT CPU baseline is multimodal with SD 31.8 ms. (2) Light memory pressure inflates TensorRT P99 from 1.28 ms to 1.61 ms; one ORT memory-stress run collapses into deterministic 198 ms regime. (3) All three TensorRT storage-stress runs produce complete software timing logs (100/100 iterations) alongside three distinct external observability failures—while the runtime reports normal completion.
AI.conclusion: Timing observability is an interference-sensitive resource; summary statistics from a single timing source can hide failure modes that an independent external observer reveals.

title: Observer-Based Stabilization for Linear Multi-Agent Dynamical Systems Using Generalized Frequency Variables
comment: 23rd IFAC World Congress, Busan, South Korea, Aug. 2026
summary: We address the conditions and design of controllers and observers for homogeneous networks of linear MIMO agents. We develop networked controllers and observers that ensure the stability of both the system state and the estimation error, leveraging the concept of generalized frequency variables. A separation principle for networks is then established, showing that the observer and controller can be designed independently and combined to achieve a stable output feedback. Our results are illustrated via a highly unstable, oscillatory network of locally actuated pendulums on carts. Finally, necessary conditions for controllability and observability -- derived from agent properties and network structure -- are established and discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper develops conditions and designs for controllers and observers in homogeneous networks of linear MIMO agents, establishes a separation principle for networks, and derives necessary controllability/observability conditions based on agent properties and network structure.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of systematic design principles for controllers and observers in networked systems, particularly ensuring stability of both system state and estimation error while enabling independent observer/controller design.
AI.method: The approach uses generalized frequency variables to design networked controllers and observers, and establishes a separation principle that allows independent design of observers and controllers combined to achieve stable output feedback.
AI.result: A separation principle for networks is established; necessary conditions for controllability and observability derived from agent properties and network structure are identified; the method is validated on an unstable oscillatory network of locally actuated pendulums on carts.
AI.conclusion: Networked controllers and observers can be designed independently using generalized frequency variables and combined via a separation principle to ensure stable output feedback for homogeneous MIMO agent networks, with necessary conditions tied to agent and network properties.

title: Residential Battery Pooling Under Backup Commitments
summary:
Residential batteries increasingly serve two roles: they can earn money by arbitraging wholesale prices and providing grid services, and they provide backup power during outages. This dual use creates a basic tradeoff between earning market value and preserving outage readiness. Coordination across many batteries can help, but a provider cannot treat the fleet as a single virtual battery when each household is promised its own backup protection.
  We compare standalone control, in which each home is dispatched independently, with pooling, in which homes are coordinated while each battery retains its own state of charge and household-specific backup requirement. Both regimes are implemented as model predictive control problems with 15-minute decision intervals and evaluated using household telemetry together with ERCOT market inputs. The empirical design focuses on the 543 homes in our sample that can support at least one backup product in standalone operation and studies backup caps ranging from 2 to 24 hours. Lower caps relax backup obligations, while the 24-hour cap coincides with assigning each home its own longest feasible backup tier.
  Pooling remains beneficial in this service-constrained setting, but its value declines smoothly as backup obligations tighten. Standalone firm margin ranges from \$11.06 per home per week at the 2-hour cap to \$10.79 at the 24-hour cap, while pooling benefit falls from \$1.49 to \$1.27 per home per week. Relative to standalone firm margin, pooling is worth about 13.5% at the 2-hour cap and about 11.8% at the 24-hour cap. Coordination therefore still helps after preserving household-level backup guarantees, but its value declines as backup obligations tighten.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the tradeoff between earning market value and preserving outage readiness in residential batteries used for both arbitrage/grid services and backup power. It compares standalone control vs. pooling (coordinated) operation under varying backup hour requirements (2-24h) using 543 homes and ERCOT data. Pooling adds value (11.8%-13.5% relative gain), but its benefit declines as backup obligations tighten.
AI.motivation: Residential batteries serve dual roles (market participation and backup power), creating a fundamental tradeoff between maximizing market value and preserving outage readiness. Coordination across batteries could help, but each household's individual backup guarantee prevents treating the fleet as a single virtual battery. The paper aims to quantify this tradeoff and the value of coordination under varying backup obligations.
AI.method: Compares standalone control (each home dispatched independently) vs. pooling (coordinated while preserving each battery's state of charge and household-specific backup requirement). Both implemented as model predictive control (MPC) problems with 15-minute decision intervals, evaluated using household telemetry and ERCOT market data. Analyzes 543 homes with backup caps from 2 to 24 hours.
AI.result: Standalone firm margin ranges from $11.06/home/week (2h cap) to $10.79/home/week (24h cap). Pooling benefit falls from $1.49 to $1.27/home/week. Relative to standalone, pooling is worth ~13.5% at 2h cap and ~11.8% at 24h cap. Pooling remains beneficial but its value declines smoothly as backup obligations tighten.
AI.conclusion: Coordination still helps after preserving household-level backup guarantees, but its value declines as backup obligations tighten. The paper quantifies the diminishing returns of pooling under increasingly stringent backup requirements.

title: Control-Certified Wireless Resource Allocation for Digital-Twin-Enabled UAV Swarms
summary:
Wireless resource allocation in digital-twin-enabled unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms must be both network-feasible and certifiably safe for closed-loop control.
  Existing packet-level or scalar-priority schedulers cannot meaningfully compare heterogeneous multi-hop actions that differ simultaneously in route, retransmission depth, blocklength, bidirectional delay, delivery probability, and TDMA slot cost.
  This paper introduces a certificate-guided resource allocation framework for low-altitude multi-hop UAV swarms.
  A digital twin maps predicted topology, channel, route, and controller-side state into a shared five-dimensional quality-of-service (QoS) certificate comprising uplink/downlink delay bounds, directional delivery guarantees, and a certified upper bound on the interval between successful bidirectional interactions.
  A state-conditioned stochastic drift test then admits only certificates whose augmented Lyapunov drift is nonpositive under the current controller state.
  Admitted actions are reduced to certified supply frontiers by removing dominated route-slot configurations, and the online scheduler maximizes Lyapunov-drift reduction under a shared TDMA slot budget via exact dynamic programming.
  Closed-loop ns-3 simulations demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms fixed-service, certificate-filtered fixed-priority, dynamic-transmission-count, and value-of-information baselines in both tracking accuracy and high-risk state suppression under identical communication budgets.

AI.tldr: A certificate-guided resource allocation framework for digital-twin-enabled multi-hop UAV swarms that ensures network-feasible and certifiably safe closed-loop control by using 5D QoS certificates, Lyapunov drift tests, and dynamic programming scheduling, outperforming baselines in tracking accuracy and high-risk state suppression.
AI.motivation: Existing packet-level or scalar-priority schedulers cannot meaningfully compare heterogeneous multi-hop actions that differ in route, retransmission depth, blocklength, bidirectional delay, delivery probability, and TDMA slot cost, yet wireless resource allocation in digital-twin-enabled UAV swarms must be both network-feasible and certifiably safe for closed-loop control.
AI.method: (1) A digital twin maps predicted topology/channel/route/controller state into a 5D QoS certificate (uplink/downlink delay bounds, directional delivery guarantees, certified upper bound on bidirectional interaction interval). (2) A state-conditioned stochastic drift test admits only certificates with nonpositive augmented Lyapunov drift. (3) Admitted actions are reduced to certified supply frontiers by removing dominated route-slot configurations. (4) An online scheduler maximizes Lyapunov-drift reduction under a shared TDMA slot budget via exact dynamic programming.
AI.result: Closed-loop ns-3 simulations show the proposed framework outperforms fixed-service, certificate-filtered fixed-priority, dynamic-transmission-count, and value-of-information baselines in both tracking accuracy and high-risk state suppression under identical communication budgets.
AI.conclusion: The certificate-guided framework enables safe and efficient resource allocation for multi-hop UAV swarms by bridging digital twin predictions with Lyapunov-based control-theoretic scheduling, delivering superior closed-loop performance.

title: Cooperative and Noncooperative Paradigms for Game-Theoretic Control of Socio-Technical Systems
summary: This tutorial presents cooperative and noncooperative game-theoretic frameworks for modeling, learning, and control in socio-technical systems, where human behavior, incentives, institutions, and social interactions are coupled with cyber-physical and networked infrastructures. The paper reviews strategic, dynamic, cooperative, matching, learning, and feedback-control approaches for analyzing how local decision-making, adaptation, and strategic interactions shape collective system outcomes. The tutorial further develops feedback-learning and incentive-design perspectives that connect equilibrium analysis with adaptation, distributed control, and mechanism design under information and coordination constraints. We also examine resilience and security challenges arising from adversarial behavior, misinformation, disruptions, and cascading failures in interconnected socio-technical networks. Finally, we discuss emerging research directions at the intersection of game theory, control, learning, and network science for resilient and adaptive socio-technical systems.

AI.tldr: This tutorial presents game-theoretic frameworks (cooperative and noncooperative) for modeling, learning, and control in socio-technical systems, covering strategic, dynamic, matching, and feedback-control approaches, with emphasis on equilibrium analysis, incentive design, resilience, and security challenges in interconnected networks.
AI.motivation: To address the coupling of human behavior, incentives, institutions, and social interactions with cyber-physical and networked infrastructures in socio-technical systems.
AI.method: Reviews strategic, dynamic, cooperative, matching, learning, and feedback-control game-theoretic approaches; develops feedback-learning and incentive-design perspectives linking equilibrium analysis with adaptation, distributed control, and mechanism design under information and coordination constraints.
AI.result: Examines resilience and security challenges from adversarial behavior, misinformation, disruptions, and cascading failures in interconnected socio-technical networks.
AI.conclusion: Discusses emerging research directions at the intersection of game theory, control, learning, and network science for resilient and adaptive socio-technical systems.

title: Learning the dynamics of nonlinear systems with regional stability guarantees through linear matrix inequality constraints
comment: This work has been accepted to IFAC for publication under a Creative Commons Licence CC-BY-NC-ND
summary: This paper presents a method that learns a regionally stable recurrent neural network model from a set of input-output data generated by an unknown dynamical system. Relying on generalized sector conditions on the deadzone activation function, we first derive sufficient conditions that guarantee forward invariance on a compact set of the state space for any inputs from a given set. Such regional properties lead to less conservative conditions compared to variants that offer a global form of stability, and are in line with the system data that is only observed regionally. Our learning method derives conditions for regional stability using a barrier function approach, leading to models equipped with a certificate of regional stability in a subset of the state space and for a given input set. We illustrate our theoretical result with a numerical example and compare it to methods that impose a global form of stability, which fail to identify the system, and with a method that imposes no stability constraints at all, which does not guarantee a stable behavior within any state or input set.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method to learn recurrent neural network models that are regionally stable—guaranteeing forward invariance on a compact state set for given inputs—using generalized sector conditions on the deadzone activation function and a barrier function approach. It is less conservative than global stability methods and more reliable than unconstrained approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing methods impose global stability, which is too conservative and often fails when learning from data observed only regionally; methods without stability constraints cannot guarantee stable behavior within any bounded region. A regional stability certificate is needed to align with limited observation data.
AI.method: The authors derive sufficient conditions for forward invariance on a compact set using generalized sector conditions on the deadzone activation function. They then formulate a learning method using a barrier function approach to enforce regional stability, producing models with a certified stable subset of the state space for a given input set.
AI.result: Numerical example demonstrates that the proposed method successfully identifies the system, whereas global stability methods fail and unconstrained methods cannot guarantee stable behavior within any input or state set.
AI.conclusion: Regionally stable RNN learning via barrier functions offers a practical middle ground: less conservative than global stability approaches and more reliable than unconstrained learning, making it suitable for data-driven modeling of unknown dynamical systems observed regionally.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging Profile Forecasting Using Hybrid Models
summary: Electric Vehicle (EV) fast charging stations require forecasting techniques both at the single charger level and aggregated level. While for the latter several models exist, forecasting individual EV charging profiles is still underexplored in literature. However, such methods may be potentially used by battery-aware scheduling, leading to a more granular update of the charging station aggregated forecast and provide a more accurate estimation of EVs departure times. Nonetheless, the variable extent of available information in time and in different settings could jeopardize these benefits. For this reason, we propose a hybrid and lightweight method to estimate the EV charging profile before and during the charging process. Besides evaluating this method on multiple EVs from a public dataset, we also assess the impact of different level of information in the time transposition of the charging profile.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid, lightweight method for estimating individual EV charging profiles at fast charging stations, addressing the underexplored problem of single-charger forecasting. It evaluates the method on public data and assesses how varying information availability impacts the time-based transposition of charging profiles.
AI.motivation: Individual EV charging profile forecasting is underexplored but crucial for battery-aware scheduling, granular forecast updates, and accurate departure time estimation. However, variable information availability across different settings could undermine these benefits.
AI.method: A hybrid, lightweight method that estimates EV charging profiles both before and during the charging process, evaluated on multiple EVs from a public dataset. The study also assesses the impact of different levels of information on the time transposition of charging profiles.
AI.result: The method is evaluated on a public dataset across multiple EVs, with analysis of how varying information levels affect the accuracy of charging profile time transposition.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid lightweight method addresses the gap in single-charger EV forecasting, with potential benefits for battery-aware scheduling and more accurate departure time estimation, though performance depends on the extent of available information.

title: Advanced PID architectures for tracking changing active constraints
summary:
Advanced regulatory control (ARC), also known as advanced PID architectures, is a simple and robust way of controlling processes with changing and possibly conflicting constraints, where it previously was believed - at least in academia - that model-based solutions, such as MPC, were the only effective solution. To illustrate this, ARC is applied in two case studies. The first is a gas-liquid separation process, in which selectors and split-parallel control are combined to achieve bidirectional inventory control in which the throughput manipulator moves automatically to the most optimal position. The second case study is on keeping acceptable air quality (CO2-level) and temperature in a room (in this case, a barn for cows). The CO2 and temperature constraints can be conflicting, leading to a hierarchical switching network of PID controllers.
  Note: this is an extended version (with simulations) of paper at IFAC World Congress, August 2026, Korea.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that Advanced Regulatory Control (ARC) with advanced PID architectures can effectively handle processes with changing/conflicting constraints, challenging the academic assumption that model-predictive control (MPC) is the only viable solution. Two case studies (gas-liquid separation and barn air quality control) validate the approach.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing academic assumption that model-based solutions like MPC are the only effective approach for processes with changing and conflicting constraints, by demonstrating that simple ARC/PID architectures can achieve comparable or superior results.
AI.method: Advanced Regulatory Control (ARC) using advanced PID architectures; Case study 1 combines selectors and split-parallel control for bidirectional inventory control in gas-liquid separation; Case study 2 employs a hierarchical switching network of PID controllers for CO2 and temperature regulation in a barn.
AI.result: ARC successfully enables bidirectional inventory control with automatic optimal throughput manipulation in gas-liquid separation; ARC maintains acceptable air quality and temperature under conflicting CO2 and temperature constraints using hierarchical PID switching in a barn environment.
AI.conclusion: Advanced PID architectures (ARC) are a simple and robust alternative to MPC for processes with changing/conflicting constraints, contrary to common academic belief. The extended version includes simulations that were not present in the original IFAC World Congress paper.

title: A characteristic function framework for chance constraint programming in stochastic model predictive control
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted by IFAC WC 2026
summary: The computation of chance constraints in stochastic model predictive control is often numerically challenging due to the non-Gaussian nature of the disturbances. To overcome this problem, we propose an optimization computational framework applicable to non-Gaussian disturbances. This framework employs a numerical inversion method, utilizing the characteristic function of the disturbance distribution to compute the probability in the chance constraint as well as its gradient. To improve efficiency, it vectorizes integral points and reuses intermediate computations in Gauss-Kronrod quadrature. The framework is implemented within the YALMIP toolbox to perform chance constraint calculations for arbitrary non-Gaussian disturbances, applicable to both single-component distributions and mixture models. It allows the user to simply specify a distribution type and its parameters for the disturbance and directly compute the probability and its gradient to solve the optimization problem. The method is validated through a numerical example of a stochastic model predictive control application.

AI.tldr: A computational framework using characteristic function inversion and Gauss-Kronrod quadrature is proposed to efficiently compute chance constraints and their gradients for non-Gaussian disturbances in stochastic MPC, implemented in YALMIP.
AI.motivation: Computing chance constraints in stochastic MPC is numerically challenging when disturbances are non-Gaussian, limiting practical applicability.
AI.method: The framework uses numerical inversion of the characteristic function of the disturbance distribution to compute probabilities and gradients. Efficiency is improved by vectorizing integral points and reusing intermediate computations in Gauss-Kronrod quadrature. It is implemented in YALMIP and supports arbitrary non-Gaussian distributions, including mixture models.
AI.result: The method is validated through a numerical example of a stochastic MPC application, demonstrating its effectiveness for chance constraint computation with non-Gaussian disturbances.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables efficient, user-friendly chance constraint handling for arbitrary non-Gaussian disturbances in stochastic MPC, requiring only specification of distribution type and parameters.

title: On Piecewise Quadratic Terminal Costs for MPC
summary: This paper presents a novel approach to synthesize stabilizing termi- nal ingredients for linear model predictive control (MPC) schemes, with the aim of increasing the region of attraction while reducing suboptimal- ity with respect to the solution of the infinite-horizon optimal control problem. It is based on the construction of a novel terminal region using methods from the field of configuration-constrained polytopic computing, along with a terminal cost that is exactly equal to the infinite-horizon linear-quadratic regulator cost in a nontrivial neighborhood of the steady- state. The practical performance of the controller is illustrated through various case studies, and comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches are presented.

AI.tldr: A method to synthesize stabilizing terminal ingredients for linear MPC using configuration-constrained polytopic computing, increasing the region of attraction and reducing suboptimality relative to infinite-horizon optimal control.
AI.motivation: To improve linear MPC by enlarging the region of attraction and reducing suboptimality compared to the infinite-horizon optimal control solution.
AI.method: Construction of a novel terminal region via configuration-constrained polytopic computing, with a terminal cost matching the infinite-horizon LQR cost in a nontrivial neighborhood of the steady-state.
AI.result: Illustrated through case studies with comparisons to state-of-the-art approaches, demonstrating improved performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed terminal ingredients effectively increase the region of attraction and reduce suboptimality in linear MPC.

title: Data Center Spatio-Temporal Load Flexibility in Security-Constrained Unit Commitment for Enhanced Grid Efficiency and Reliability
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, accepted by IEEE IAS Annual Meeting 2026
summary: Data center electricity consumption reached 4.4% of U.S. total in 2023 and is projected to grow to 6.7--12% by 2028, imposing increasing stress on transmission networks while representing a largely untapped source of controllable demand-side flexibility. This paper proposes a modular security-constrained unit commitment (SCUC) framework that coordinates flexible data center workloads with system-level scheduling to reduce renewable curtailment, alleviate congestion, and lower operating costs. Three mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models are formulated: the Data Center Spatial model (DC-S), enabling instantaneous workload redistribution across geographically distributed sites; the Data Center Temporal model (DC-T), permitting each site to shift its deferrable load across time while preserving the daily energy balance; and the Data Center Spatio-Temporal model (DC-ST), jointly activating both mechanisms and spanning the largest feasible operating region. Case studies on a modified IEEE 24-bus reliability test system show that DC-ST eliminates all base-case and post-contingency transmission violations at a flexibility ratio of 40%, and reduces renewable curtailment by up to 84.4% at 30% relative to the inflexible baseline. Sensitivity analysis further reveals that moderate flexibility levels of 20%--30% already capture most of the achievable benefits, supporting practical deployment with limited operational burden on data center operators.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a modular SCUC framework integrating flexible data center workloads (spatial, temporal, or spatio-temporal) to reduce renewable curtailment, alleviate congestion, and lower operating costs, with the spatio-temporal model (DC-ST) eliminating all transmission violations at 40% flexibility and reducing curtailment by up to 84.4%.
AI.motivation: Data center electricity consumption is rapidly growing (4.4% of U.S. total in 2023, projected 6.7–12% by 2028), stressing transmission networks while offering untapped controllable demand-side flexibility.
AI.method: Three MILP models (DC-S for spatial redistribution, DC-T for temporal load shifting, DC-ST combining both) are formulated and integrated into a modular SCUC framework.
AI.result: DC-ST eliminates all base-case and post-contingency violations at 40% flexibility; reduces renewable curtailment by up to 84.4% at 30% flexibility; 20–30% flexibility captures most benefits.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating data center workload flexibility with system-level scheduling significantly enhances grid reliability and renewable integration, with moderate flexibility levels sufficient for practical deployment.

title: HJ-Gauss: A Monte-Carlo HJ Reachability Scheme
summary: Backward reachable tubes (BRTs), computed via viscous Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) partial differential equations, provide principled safety certificates for learned controllers and planning algorithms in trustworthy machine learning. However, classical grid-based HJ solvers require $O(M^n)$ memory footprint for $M$ grid points per $n$ state dimension. This renders them impractical for high-dimensional systems. We address this bottleneck with a local PDE linearization that enables a frozen-coefficient sampling scheme for the viscous HJ PDE: a generalized Cole-Hopf-type transformation reduces the nonlinear HJ equation to a sequence of linear heat equations whose solutions admit Gaussian heat-kernel representations. The value function and its spatial gradient are then recovered via roll-outs of Monte Carlo expectations on Gaussian densities, yielding a storage and grid-free algorithm that scales as $N\cdot n$ for $N$ samples. This decoupling of memory from dimensionality enables reachability analysis on problems where grid-based methods are simply impossible. We prove a finite-sample concentration bound $O(N^{-1/2})$ error and conditional linear convergence for the introduced Monte-Carlo Picard iterative scheme. Numerical validation on pursuit-evasion games demonstrates relative $L^2_{\text{rel}}$ errors of $0.03 - 0.20$, with $14-26$ second wall-clock times per 2D slice on a CPU. Crucially, the method scales with validation on up to (but not limited to) $n=45$-dimensional multi-agent games.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a grid-free Monte Carlo method for computing backward reachable tubes (BRTs) via a generalized Cole-Hopf transformation that reduces the viscous HJ PDE to linear heat equations solvable by Gaussian sampling, achieving O(N·n) memory scaling and proving O(N^{-1/2}) convergence, with demonstrations up to 45-dimensional systems.
AI.motivation: Classical grid-based HJ solvers require O(M^n) memory, making BRT computation intractable for high-dimensional systems, thus limiting principled safety certification in trustworthy machine learning.
AI.method: A local PDE linearization via a generalized Cole-Hopf-type transformation reduces the nonlinear viscous HJ equation to a sequence of linear heat equations; their solutions admit Gaussian heat-kernel representations, enabling Monte Carlo sampling roll-outs that recover the value function and its spatial gradient with O(N·n) storage.
AI.result: Finite-sample concentration bound of O(N^{-1/2}) error and conditional linear convergence for the Picard iterative scheme; numerical validation on pursuit-evasion games shows relative L² errors of 0.03-0.20 with 14-26 second wall-clock times per 2D slice on CPU, and scaling demonstrated up to 45-dimensional multi-agent games.
AI.conclusion: The proposed grid-free algorithm decouples memory from dimensionality, enabling reachability analysis on high-dimensional problems where grid-based methods are infeasible, with provable convergence guarantees.

title: Comparing Contract-Based Support Mechanisms for Long-Duration Energy Storage
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 22nd International Conference on the European Energy Market (EEM26), Trondheim, Norway, 2026
summary: Long-duration energy storage (LDES) faces significant revenue volatility that impedes investment. This paper evaluates four contract-based support mechanisms using an equilibrium model with risk-averse investors and incomplete risk markets. Applied to a stylized 2035 Great Britain case, we find that all mechanisms can achieve the targeted LDES capacity but differ substantially in cost-effectiveness and risk-aversion sensitivity. Contracts that eliminate revenue volatility achieve the lowest costs but may weaken operational incentives, while contracts that preserve market exposure maintain incentives at higher costs.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates four contract-based support mechanisms for long-duration energy storage (LDES) using an equilibrium model with risk-averse investors and incomplete risk markets, applied to a 2035 Great Britain case. It finds that all mechanisms achieve target LDES capacity but differ in cost-effectiveness and sensitivity to risk aversion, with trade-offs between eliminating revenue volatility (lower cost, weaker incentives) and preserving market exposure (higher cost, stronger incentives).
AI.motivation: Long-duration energy storage (LDES) faces significant revenue volatility that impedes investment, motivating the need for contract-based support mechanisms to de-risk investment while maintaining operational efficiency.
AI.method: The paper develops an equilibrium model incorporating risk-averse investors and incomplete risk markets. It evaluates four contract-based support mechanisms applied to a stylized 2035 Great Britain case.
AI.result: All four mechanisms achieve the targeted LDES capacity but differ substantially in cost-effectiveness and sensitivity to risk aversion. Contracts eliminating revenue volatility achieve lowest costs but weaken operational incentives, while contracts preserving market exposure maintain incentives at higher costs.
AI.conclusion: There is an inherent trade-off in LDES support mechanism design: mechanisms that fully hedge revenue risk are more cost-effective for achieving capacity targets but dull operational incentives, whereas mechanisms retaining market risk exposure preserve incentives at the expense of higher overall costs.

title: Robust Soft-Constrained Spatially Selective Active Noise Control for Hearables Under Secondary Path Variations
comment: Submitted to the 19th International Workshop on Acoustic Signal Enhancement (IWAENC 2026)
summary: Spatially selective active noise control (SSANC) hearables aim to attenuate noise from certain directions at the eardrum while preserving desired speech arriving from selected directions. Existing SSANC systems typically assume an accurate estimate of the secondary path from the loudspeaker to the inner error microphone. In practice, however, this path varies across users and device fits, which can degrade performance and compromise system stability. This paper proposes a robust soft-constrained optimization framework that computes a single control filter by minimizing the average cost over a set of secondary path estimates derived from human measurements. Simulations and experiments on a real-time control platform show that the proposed approach slightly reduces mean performance relative to the matched case but substantially narrows the performance spread under secondary path mismatch. The proposed framework therefore provides a practical design strategy when accurate secondary path estimates are unavailable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a robust soft-constrained optimization framework for SSANC hearables that computes a single control filter by minimizing average cost over multiple secondary path estimates from human measurements, reducing performance variability under path mismatch at the cost of slightly lower mean performance.
AI.motivation: Existing SSANC systems assume accurate secondary path estimates from loudspeaker to error microphone, but this path varies across users and device fits, causing performance degradation and stability issues.
AI.method: A robust soft-constrained optimization framework that computes a single control filter by minimizing the average cost over a set of secondary path estimates derived from human measurements.
AI.result: The approach slightly reduces mean performance compared to the matched case but substantially narrows the performance spread under secondary path mismatch, validated by simulations and real-time experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a practical design strategy for SSANC hearables when accurate secondary path estimates are unavailable.
